notes:
I covered most verses, but there are gaps. I found nothing usable for vv. 17 and 29, and nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace sites, so those are left out. Protestant teachers really differ only at vv. 26–28. My searches ran out before I could check enduringword's later sections (vv. 18–20) or the NET notes directly; the NET points below come second-hand through Precept Austin and Bible.org.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says Og attacked without provocation… either disliking the presence of such dangerous neighbours, or burning to avenge the overthrow of his friends and allies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/deuteronomy-3.html)
- Precept Austin notes that, as with Sihon, Og left his fortified city to meet Israel in the open. It calls this arrogance, since he must have heard what happened to Sihon. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-3-commentary)
- Utley says the "road" was the King's Highway, a major caravan route. Og probably used the river at Edrei as his defensive line. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)

**v. 2**
- Guzik: God told Israel not to fear Og despite his size, and promised the same victory as over the Amorites. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)
- JFB: Og belonged to a doomed race and is destined to share the fate of Sihon. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_003.cfm)
- Utley counts how often "give" appears in these chapters and concludes that YHWH is the giver. He calls the setting "holy war". (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)

**v. 3**
- Precept Austin calls this total destruction typical of holy war. It notes the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) says none of Og's descendants were left, so his family line ended for good. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-3-commentary)

**v. 4**
- Guzik: this victory showed Israel that, by God's power, they could beat the Canaanites west of the Jordan. He quotes Kalland that "cities" could mean places of only a few hundred people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)

**v. 5**
- Utley: the cities were built of volcanic stone and looked intimidating, but Israel's faith was stronger than its fear of the giants. "Gates and bars" may mean a double gate with a metal bar. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)
- JFB: these buildings of black basalt were almost as hard as iron. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/deuteronomy-3.html)

**vv. 6–7**
- Utley: the Hebrew word means devoting something to God so that it becomes too holy for human use and must be destroyed. He lists three kinds of "ban"; this verse is the kind where the people die but the cattle are kept. In his view the Canaanites were judged for their sins and refusal to repent. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)
- Gill: it was the people who were destroyed, not the cities, which Israel took over and lived in. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/deuteronomy/3-6.html)
- The BibleHub study note says the ban was meant to keep Israel from being drawn into Canaanite idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/3-6.htm)

**v. 8**
- Utley sets this verse beside v. 24, where it is God's "strong hand" that wins. He sees God's sovereignty and human effort working together. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)

**v. 9**
- Utley thinks "Sidonians" (rather than Tyre) and "Sirion" (found in Ugaritic texts) point to an ancient text. "Senir" appears in records of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)

**v. 10**
- Utley: "the plateau" is the tableland between the Arnon and Heshbon, which went to Reuben. Salecah marks the south-eastern edge of Bashan. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)

**v. 11**
- Guzik: the bed was about 14 by 6 feet, whether bed or coffin. The repeated mentions of the Rephaim show that Israel's fear of them 40 years earlier was unfounded. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)
- The Geneva Study Bible note: The more terrible this giant was, the greater reason they had to glorify God for the victory. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/3-11.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch say Moses mentions the bed to recall God's grace in the victory. Barnes thinks the "iron" was probably black basalt. (Same page.)
- Matthew Henry: Og trusted his own strength, and so was hardened to his destruction. (Same page.)
- Clarke: iron was used for strength and to keep out vermin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/3-11.html)
- How did the bed reach Rabbah? Gill suggests Og sent it there for safety, or Israel sold it to the Ammonites. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/3-11.htm)

**vv. 12–13**
- Guzik: the repeated "I gave" shows the land was God's to hand out as He chose. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)
- Utley: Reuben and Gad took over Sihon's kingdom, and Manasseh's share was split across the Jordan. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)

**v. 14**
- JFB: Jair named the towns "Jair's Bedouin Villages of Tents." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_003.cfm)
- Gill: Geshur and Maacah were small Syrian kingdoms that Israel never took. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/3-14.html)
- Utley: "son of" here means "descendant of". (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)
- For the dispute over "to this day", see the scholarship section below.

**vv. 18–20**
- Guzik: Moses is recalling the deal in Numbers 32, and the eastern tribes kept it honourably (Joshua 22). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)

**vv. 21–22**
- Guzik: remembering God's past faithfulness was key to Joshua's trust. He quotes Morgan: it does not so much mean that God was on their side, as that they were on the side of God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)

**vv. 23–25**
- Guzik: "pleaded" is a strong word, and Moses knew it did no harm to ask God to relent. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)
- R.M. Edgar: it was natural for Moses to want to finish his life's work. (https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/edgar/moses'_longing_to_enter_the_promised_land_refused.htm)

**v. 26**
- Barnes: here Moses blames the people's sin, while elsewhere the blame is his own. The difference is because Moses is speaking to the people here, as a warning to them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/3-26.htm)
- Ellicott quotes Rashi's reading of "let it suffice thee": much more good is stored up for Moses. (Same page.)
- Guzik: God says no even to His greatest intercessors. Leaders are judged more strictly (James 3:1). At Meribah Moses spoiled a picture of Christ, the Rock struck only once. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)

**v. 27**
- Guzik, quoting Kalland: Pisgah is probably Ras es-Siyaghah, with a view over all of Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)
- GotQuestions sees compassion in God showing Moses the land before he died. (https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-promised-land.html)

**v. 28**
- Guzik: Moses still had to help his successor succeed, an example for leaders today. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-3/)

## Where Protestant traditions differ (vv. 26–28)

- **Reformed (Calvin):** He disagrees with those who think God was offended by Moses' longing. Moses is rather giving the reason why he did not obtain what he sought, viz., because he had been already excluded from it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/3-26.html)
- **Baptist / Calvinist (Gill):** God's anger was not over this prayer but over Meribah. (Same page.)
- **Puritan (Matthew Henry):** Even people delivered from the wrath to come may yet lie under the tokens of God's wrath in this world. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_003.cfm)
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** This is a matter of law and gospel. Moses stands for the law, which could never get the people of God to the promised land. (https://www.1517.org/articles/the-law-cannot-enter-the-promised-land)
- **Typology debate:** Unger reads "for your sakes" as a picture of Christ bearing wrath for the people. Coffman rejects any vicarious meaning; for him God's impartiality is the point. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/3-26.html)
- **Joshua as a picture of Christ:** Guzik quotes a writer: what Moses' law could not do, Christ by his gospel hath done for us. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

## Other views

**Modern scholarship, v. 11:**
- The NET note says the "bed" is likely a basalt sarcophagus (stone coffin) whose iron-like look got it called iron. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-3-commentary)
- Utley adds that one reference work finds "no literary support" for the sarcophagus idea. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-3)
- Keil calls the sarcophagus view improbable. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/3-11.htm)

**"To this day", v. 14 (and v. 11) — who wrote it?**
- Benson and Poole think the phrase was added by later editors. JFB suggests Ezra. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/3-14.htm)
- Ellicott suggests Joshua. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/3-14.html)
- One commentary on the BibleHub page calls the note a "harmonising insertion" based on Numbers 32:41.
- Keil disagrees: the phrase certainly does not point to a later period than the Mosaic age. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/3-14.htm)
